case_brief.incident_description: Naledi had worked for the agency for three years. She told her manager that she was pregnant and two weeks later was informed that her role was redundant. She says the business had recently won two new clients, that another junior employee in the same team was retained, and that she received no written section 189(3) notice or meaningful consultation before the decision. She was offered one month notice and severance. The employer described the decision as restructuring.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: I told my manager I was pregnant and two weeks later they retrenched me. We had just won two new clients. The junior in my team stayed and nobody consulted with me before telling me my job was gone.
case_brief.recommended_next_step: Urgent WP letter challenging the retrenchment process and raising the pregnancy-linked dismissal risk.
weaknesses: Employer may produce financial or restructuring evidence not yet seen

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Ms Naledi Dlamini, in connection with the termination of her employment with Orbit Creative Agency (Pty) Ltd. This letter is written without prejudice and subject to contract, with all of our client's rights expressly reserved to proceed to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration or any other appropriate forum without further notice should a satisfactory resolution not be reached. Nothing in this letter constitutes an admission of fact or liability on the part of our client.

2. Our client disclosed to her manager that she was pregnant. Approximately two weeks later she was informed that her role had been identified as redundant and that her employment was being terminated by way of what the employer characterised as restructuring. Our client was offered one month's notice and severance pay.

3. To the extent that our client's account is confirmed, no written notice in terms of section 189(3) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 was issued to her prior to the decision being communicated, and no meaningful consultation process preceded the termination. Our client records that the business had recently secured two new clients at or around the time of her dismissal. Our client also records, conditionally and for completeness only, that another junior colleague in her team was retained; we do not at this stage advance this as an established comparator, since the role, duties, performance and tenure of that colleague relative to our client's position have not been confirmed, and it is recorded here purely as a fact our client reports.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: substantive and procedural fairness under section 188(1) of the LRA: Our client's dismissal falls to be assessed first against section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act, which requires a dismissal to be for a fair reason and effected in accordance with a fair procedure. The Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 is the applicable instrument and, where retrenchment is advanced as the stated reason, paragraphs 22 to 24 of the Code apply alongside sections 189 and 189A of the LRA. On the facts as reported, our client was not issued with a written notice under section 189(3) setting out the reasons for the proposed retrenchment, the alternatives considered, the proposed selection criteria or severance terms, and no meaningful consultation process took place before the decision was communicated to her. Our client's position is that the absence of any section 189(3) notice and the absence of consultation are substantial procedural defects going to the heart of the fairness enquiry, and that the employer will be required to account for them. It is material to record that our client understands the business had recently secured two new clients at or around the time of her dismissal, which calls into question whether the operational requirement relied upon was genuine. The employer's characterisation of the process as restructuring does not, without a documented and consulted process, establish that the reason was genuine or that dismissal was the fair outcome.

2. Automatically unfair dismissal: pregnancy under section 187(1)(e) of the LRA: Our client's dismissal followed her disclosure of her pregnancy to her manager by a period of approximately two weeks. We view this timing, combined with the absence of any section 189(3) notice and the absence of meaningful consultation, as giving rise to a strong inference that the true reason for her dismissal was connected to her pregnancy, which would render the dismissal automatically unfair under section 187(1)(e) of the LRA. An automatically unfair dismissal on this ground is not subject to the ordinary 12-month compensation cap under section 194(1); compensation of up to 24 months' remuneration is available under section 194(3) where this ground is established. We record, for completeness and strictly on a conditional basis, our client's account that another junior colleague in her team was retained; we do not treat this as a confirmed comparator for the purposes of this claim, given that the role, duties and tenure of that colleague have not been established, and it is not relied upon here as an independent evidential proposition. The convergence of the procedural defects identified above with the proximity in time between the pregnancy disclosure and the dismissal is, in our client's position, a matter that will be pursued should a negotiated resolution not be reached.

3. Notice entitlement under sections 37 and 38 of the BCEA: Our client was offered one month's notice. To the extent that the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, or under her contract of employment, exceeds that offered, our client's position is that payment in lieu of the applicable notice period is sought under section 38 of the BCEA, with the applicable notice period itself determined under section 37. Our client reserves her position fully in this regard pending confirmation of the applicable period.

4. Severance entitlement under section 41 of the BCEA: Separately, our client was offered severance pay. Severance pay, to the extent not already fully discharged, remains due under section 41 of the BCEA by reference to our client's completed years of continuous service, which is to be confirmed. Our client's position is that any severance already tendered must be verified against this statutory entitlement before it can be treated as having been correctly discharged.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without derogating from the position set out above, and in the interests of reaching a swift and amicable resolution, our client proposes that the matter be resolved on the following terms:

• Ex gratia compensation on a total cost to company basis, calibrated within the framework of compensation of up to 24 months' remuneration available under section 194(3) of the LRA. Our client's position is that the convergence of the absence of a section 189(3) notice, the absence of meaningful consultation and the proximity between the pregnancy disclosure and the dismissal justifies a substantial settlement figure proportionate to this exposure.

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Confirmation that any severance pay due under section 41 of the BCEA has been correctly calculated and paid in full by reference to our client's completed years of service.

• Payment of any accrued but untaken leave pay owed under section 40 of the BCEA.

• Confirmation that pension or provident fund contributions, if applicable, are paid up to date and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the relevant fund.

• Confirmation that UIF contributions are paid up to date and provision of a completed UI-19 certificate.

• Issue of a certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA.

• An agreed written reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties.

• An undertaking by the employer and its representatives not to disparage our client in any communication with third parties.

• Confidentiality as to the terms of settlement, the negotiations and the existence of this dispute as between the parties and their respective advisers.

• The terms of settlement to be reduced to a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved until such agreement is signed.

Our client's claims, taken together, present material exposure for the employer, both in respect of the procedural requirements of sections 189 and 189A of the LRA and in respect of the automatically unfair dismissal framework under section 187(1)(e). Our client's position is that a negotiated resolution is in the interests of both parties, and we invite Orbit Creative Agency (Pty) Ltd to engage constructively with the proposal set out above.

We invite a substantive response within seven calendar days of the date of this letter, failing which our client's instructions are to proceed to refer this matter to the CCMA for conciliation and, if necessary, arbitration, without further notice. All of our client's rights are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The comparator fact (junior colleague retained) is appropriately hedged as conditional and not relied upon as an established comparator, which is good discipline. However, the draft introduces 'at or around the time of her dismissal' for the new-client win without this qualifier being in the brief (brief only says 'recently won two new clients', no explicit timing link to dismissal date) and the severance paragraph speculates that tendered severance may not have been 'correctly discharged' without any brief support that the severance offered was miscalculated or incomplete. Both are mild unsupported inferences presented as live issues rather than clearly flagged open questions.
criteria.required_fix: Remove or soften the 'at or around the time of her dismissal' temporal gloss on the new-clients fact to match the brief's looser framing, and reframe the severance paragraph to request confirmation of the calculation rather than implying a doubt not evidenced in the brief.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'our client understands the business had recently secured two new clients at or around the time of her dismissal' and 'any severance already tendered must be verified against this statutory entitlement before it can be treated as having been correctly discharged'

criteria.problem: The draft correctly anchors retrenchment procedural defects (no s189(3) notice, no consultation) and the pregnancy-timing AUD claim, consistent with the HIGH merit band and override flags. It appropriately avoids overclaiming the comparator. One gap: the brief's SHAM_RETRENCHMENT flag and the 'questionable selection' scoring component are addressed via the new-clients point but the draft does not explicitly connect the retained junior colleague's continued employment to the sham-retrenchment inference even in a hedged way, slightly underusing an available (though comparator-disciplined) strategic point.
criteria.required_fix: Add a sentence noting that the fact of a colleague's retention is recorded as a further matter the employer will be expected to explain in the context of the operational requirement, without asserting it as a comparator.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: the draft treats the retained-colleague fact as 'not relied upon as an independent evidential proposition' entirely, rather than flagging it as a further line of inquiry strengthening the sham-retrenchment theory

criteria.problem: Tone is controlled, professional and counterparty-appropriate per the Counterparty-Facing profile, uses restrained formulations ('Our client's position is', 'It is material to record'). No major violations. Minor stylistic point: repeated use of 'Our client's position is' across multiple paragraphs borders on a repeated-opener pattern the house style anti-detection discipline warns against.
criteria.required_fix: Vary the phrasing used to introduce the client's position across paragraphs to avoid a repeated topic-label opener.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'Our client's position is that the absence of any section 189(3) notice...' and 'Our client's position is that payment in lieu...' and 'Our client's position is that any severance already tendered...'

criteria.problem: Claims are distinct and well-headed, progression from facts to law to settlement is logical. The notice and severance claims are somewhat thin/templated and slightly repeat conditional qualifiers ('to the extent', 'our client's position is') in a formulaic way across short paragraphs, reducing some natural variation expected under house style.
criteria.required_fix: Tighten and vary phrasing in the notice and severance paragraphs so they read less templated.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Notice and severance claim paragraphs are short and each ends with a near-identical reservation formula.

criteria.problem: Settlement terms follow the standing order substantially, are narrative and cap-relative, no rand figures, response window is seven calendar days which is compliant. Minor: the ex gratia clause justifies quantum by reference to procedural and substantive factors appropriately calibrated to HIGH merit without overstating certainty.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'We invite a substantive response within seven calendar days of the date of this letter'

criteria.problem: The first Code reference reads 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' which satisfies the mandatory current-law check for the misconduct/retrenchment analysis paragraph. However, the BCEA notice-pay clause in settlement_terms uses 'Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA ... such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked' which is one of the two expressly compliant formulations and should not be penalised. No Schedule 8 reference, no case law, no rand figures, no disparagement mutuality issue (one-way undertaking only against employer). No disciplinary charge misattribution. No PIP references present. The retrenchment claim correctly anchors in LRA s188(1) before applying the Code. On balance this criterion is largely compliant; the only residual concern is the earlier-flagged speculative severance-discharge language, which borders on an unsupported assertion that the severance may be incorrect without brief support, a mild safety/overstatement concern rather than a hard compliance breach.
criteria.required_fix: Reframe to a neutral request for confirmation of the severance calculation rather than implying unconfirmed doubt about correctness.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'Our client's position is that any severance already tendered must be verified against this statutory entitlement before it can be treated as having been correctly discharged.'

what_is_strong: Comparator discipline is handled correctly: the retained junior colleague fact is expressly flagged as conditional and not relied upon as an established comparator, avoiding the unsupported-expansion trap.

The pregnancy-linked AUD claim under section 187(1)(e) is properly connected to the procedural defects (no s189(3) notice, no consultation) rather than asserted in isolation, giving a coherent causal narrative.
Settlement clauses follow the standing 3A.10 order substantially, remain narrative and cap-relative with no itemised rand figures, and the response window is compliant at seven calendar days.
The notice-pay clause correctly treats BCEA sections 37 and 38 as complementary rather than alternative provisions.
Non-disparagement undertaking is correctly one-way against the employer, consistent with employee-side convention and no mutuality authorisation in the brief.
what_needs_work: The 'at or around the time of her dismissal' temporal gloss on the new-clients fact slightly overstates the brief's looser framing and should be softened.
The severance paragraph implies unconfirmed doubt about correctness of payment already tendered without brief support for that doubt; this should be reframed as a neutral confirmation request.
Repeated use of 'Our client's position is' as a paragraph opener across multiple claims borders on the repeated topic-label pattern the house style anti-detection discipline flags.
The notice and severance claim paragraphs are templated and could be tightened and varied for a more natural register.

Consider whether the retained colleague's continued employment should be noted (still without comparator status) as a further matter requiring employer explanation, to fully capture the sham-retrenchment angle supported by the override flag.
risks_to_monitor: Employer may produce documentary evidence of a genuine operational rationale or financial pressure not yet seen by VRS, which could weaken the sham-retrenchment and AUD inference.
The conditional language around the comparator and new-clients timing, if challenged, needs to be defensible as genuinely unconfirmed rather than a hedge masking a stronger assertion.
CCMA referral window has 20 days remaining; any delay in employer engagement could compress the Client's options before the 30-day limit.
forensic_questions: What exact date did Ms Dlamini disclose her pregnancy to her manager, and what date was she told her role was redundant, to confirm the two-week proximity precisely?
What were the role, seniority, tenure and performance record of the junior colleague who was retained, to assess whether a comparator case can later be properly constructed?
On what date(s) did Orbit Creative Agency publicly announce or internally confirm the two new client wins, relative to the dismissal date?
Was any verbal or informal consultation attempted by the employer that has not yet been disclosed to VRS, and if so when and with whom?
What is the breakdown of the severance amount already offered, and against what years-of-service calculation was it derived, to verify compliance with BCEA section 41?
Does Ms Dlamini have a written employment contract specifying a notice period longer than the BCEA section 37 minimum?

criteria.problem: The comparator is expanded beyond what the brief supports: the draft repeatedly treats the retained junior colleague as a meaningful comparator ('our client will rely upon in support of the proposition') without flagging that same team or junior status does not establish same/similar role or that pregnancy was the sole material difference. Additionally the two new clients fact is stated as 'our client records' / 'our client understands' which is acceptably conditional, but the comparator framing crosses from conditional record-keeping into an affirmative evidentiary argument ('is a matter our client will rely upon in support of the proposition that the stated operational reason does not fully account for the timing'). No invented names, dates or salary figures are present, and the generic incident_date is not misassigned to a specific sub-event, which is a positive.
criteria.required_fix: Keep the comparator strictly conditional throughout; do not convert the unconfirmed comparator into a supporting proposition for causation in the legal claims section until role/duties/tenure are confirmed. Add explicit comparator-discipline caveat in the legal claim text itself, not only in the background paragraph.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "We note this comparator conditionally... given that the precise role, duties and tenure of that colleague relative to our client's position have not yet been confirmed" immediately followed in the AUD claim by "is a matter our client will rely upon in support of the proposition that the stated operational reason does not fully account for the timing and manner of her dismissal."

criteria.problem: The draft understates the merits relative to the deterministic HIGH band (substantive 9, procedural 10) by hedging excessively on causation ('raises a live question', 'our respectful submission') for a matter the brief treats as a strong sham-retrenchment/pregnancy case with multiple overlapping triggers (no s189(3) notice, no consultation, pregnancy timing, questionable selection). The unfair dismissal claim is framed under section 188(1) read with Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 and ss189/189A as required, and the AUD claim correctly invokes section 187(1)(e) and the 24-month cap, which is good. However the settlement ex gratia clause, while connecting to the risk factors, uses soft language ('our client's position is that a substantial settlement figure is warranted') without clearly tying it to the HIGH merit band's calibration above the midpoint of the cap, which somewhat underplays the leverage the brief supports.
criteria.required_fix: Firm up the causal language to reflect the strength of the stacked facts (no notice, no consultation, timing, retained junior, new clients) while remaining non-hyperbolic; avoid unnecessary hedges like 'our respectful submission' which dilute a strong procedural case; ensure the settlement clause explicitly ties the proposed figure to the convergence of the s189 defects and the pregnancy-linked timing to justify a stronger calibration consistent with HIGH band without quoting a rand figure.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "This temporal proximity raises a live question as to whether the true reason for her dismissal was connected to her pregnancy" and "in our respectful submission, significant procedural defects" versus the brief's substantive_score 9/procedural_score 10 and merit_band HIGH with stacked triggers (no notice, no consultation, pregnancy proximity, questionable selection).

criteria.problem: Tone is largely professional and controlled but contains hedging formulations inconsistent with the confident, authoritative counterparty-facing register required by the audience profile ('in our respectful submission', 'raises a live question', 'our client's understanding'). These soften a matter that the deterministic scoring treats as strong, undercutting the 'authority through precision and certainty' standard. No prohibited stock-aggressive phrases are used, which is good, and overall restraint is appropriate.
criteria.required_fix: Replace deferential hedges with firmer, still proportionate formulations drawn from the house style register (e.g. 'Our client's position is that...', 'We view this timing as...', 'It is material to record that...') to project the controlled authority expected on a HIGH-merit matter.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "in our respectful submission, significant procedural defects"; "This temporal proximity raises a live question as to whether the true reason..."

criteria.problem: The structure is logical: background, then three clearly separated numbered legal claims with concise headings, then settlement intro, settlement terms, and conclusion. No duplicated template content and no duplicate salutation/closing elements appear in the body (consistent with the scope rule that the chassis supplies those). One minor readability issue is that the severance and notice claim combines two distinct entitlements (notice shortfall and severance) under one heading without a clear internal signpost separating them, which slightly blurs the single-topic-per-paragraph convention.
criteria.required_fix: Split the notice entitlement and severance entitlement into two short paragraphs, or add a clear in-paragraph signpost separating the two topics for readability.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: The claim titled 'Severance and notice entitlements' merges both section 37/38 notice analysis and section 41 severance analysis in one undifferentiated paragraph.

criteria.problem: The settlement terms are clear, follow the standing 3A.10 order reasonably well (ex gratia, notice, severance, leave, pension/provident, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, clean record, agreement to follow) and the response window is seven calendar days, which is compliant. The only soft point is the 'clean record/expungement' clause which is included even though there is no confirmed disciplinary finding on the facts, introduced with 'to the extent that', which is conditionally appropriate but arguably unnecessary surplusage for a pure retrenchment matter; this is a minor proportionality issue rather than a compliance breach.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the clean-record/expungement clause or confirm it only if a disciplinary record issue is actually in play; it is not supported by the retrenchment-only facts in the brief and may be struck as surplus unless the caseworker confirms relevance.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "To the extent that any adverse disciplinary finding or outcome exists on our client's personnel record arising from this matter, confirmation that it will be expunged..." invited despite no disciplinary process being in the brief.

criteria.problem: No case-law citations, no rand figures, no duplicate salutation/closing/signature content (correctly outside Part A scope), no Schedule 8 references, and the Code citation correctly identifies 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' on first reference. The BCEA notice-pay treatment is compliant under the mandatory check (section 38 payment in lieu with section 37 period, treated as complementary, not alternatives). No disciplinary charge is attributed to a manager beyond what is confirmed. No improper PIP claims. No unsupported evidence-possession claims.
criteria.required_fix: No fix required; maintain this compliance in the redraft.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "payment in lieu of the applicable notice period is sought under section 38 of the BCEA, with the applicable notice period determined under section 37" correctly pairs the two sections; "Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025" is used throughout, not a bare or Schedule 8 reference.

what_is_strong: Correct current-law Code citation ('Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025') used consistently with no Schedule 8 references.
BCEA sections 37 and 38 treated as complementary, consistent with the mandatory current-law check.
Settlement clauses substantially follow the standing 3A.10 order and stay within the seven-calendar-day response window.
AUD claim correctly invokes section 187(1)(e) and accurately states the 24-month cap under section 194(3) rather than conflating it with the 12-month cap.
No invented names, salary figures or case-law citations; conditional wording is used for the unconfirmed comparator record.
what_needs_work: Comparator discipline: the retained junior colleague is used as a supporting proposition in the AUD claim beyond the conditional caveat given in the background, which is an unsupported factual expansion.

Causation and procedural-defect language is overly hedged ('raises a live question', 'in our respectful submission') for a HIGH merit band matter with stacked procedural and substantive triggers, understating the leverage the facts support.
The notice/severance claim paragraph merges two distinct BCEA entitlements without clear separation, slightly reducing readability.
The clean-record/expungement settlement clause is included without any disciplinary-finding fact in the brief, introducing unsupported surplusage.
Tone throughout the legal claims is more tentative than the counterparty-facing 'authority through precision and certainty' standard requires.
risks_to_monitor: If the comparator is later shown to differ materially in role or tenure, the AUD claim's reliance on it as support could be challenged by the employer as speculative.
Employer may produce financial/restructuring evidence rebutting the operational-requirement challenge, as flagged in the brief's weaknesses.
The seven-day response window combined with hedged causation language may reduce negotiating leverage despite the strong underlying merit band.
Inclusion of an unsupported clean-record clause could invite employer scrutiny of drafting rigour and undermine credibility on the stronger claims.
forensic_questions: What is the role, seniority, tenure and specific duties of the retained junior colleague relative to the client's position, to confirm or rebut comparator equivalence?
What is the exact date the client's manager was told of the pregnancy, and through what medium, to firm up the causal proximity argument?
Is there any documentary evidence (e-mail, memo, minutes) recording the business securing the two new clients, and the date of that development relative to the dismissal?
Was any alternative role or redeployment considered or available at the time of the retrenchment decision, and if so what happened to it?
Does the client have a copy of the termination letter or any written communication from the employer describing the restructuring rationale?
initial_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is substantively sound on the mandatory current-law and BCEA compliance checks (correct Code citation, s37/s38 notice-pay treatment, correct AUD cap, no Schedule 8 or case-law citations, no rand figures) and follows the required body order and settlement-clause structure. However it falls below the 7.5 floor because it over-hedges the causal and procedural analysis for a HIGH-merit, substantively strong matter, expands the unconfirmed comparator into a supporting proposition in the AUD claim contrary to comparator discipline, merges two distinct BCEA entitlements in one paragraph, and includes an unsupported clean-record/expungement clause not grounded in the brief. These are correctable defects rather than wholesale redraft issues, but they require a further drafting pass before the letter is ready to send.
recommended_amendments: Strengthen causal and procedural-defect language consistent with the HIGH merit band while keeping it proportionate and non-hyperbolic; remove unnecessary deference such as 'in our respectful submission'.
Confine the comparator reference to clearly conditional language in both the background and the AUD claim; do not treat it as a supporting proposition until role and tenure are confirmed.
Split the notice and severance entitlement content into two distinct short paragraphs or add a clear internal signpost.
Remove or properly condition the clean-record/expungement clause, which is not supported by the retrenchment-only fact pattern in the brief.

supervisory_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is substantively sound and reflects the HIGH merit band and override flags (pregnancy, sham retrenchment, no consultation) without overstating certainty, and correctly exercises comparator discipline by not elevating the retained-colleague fact into an established comparator. Residual issues are minor: a slightly overstated temporal gloss on the new-clients fact, an unsupported implication of doubt about the severance payment's correctness, and some repetitive phrasing across claim paragraphs. These are drafting polish issues rather than mandatory-check failures, so the floor is met at 8.0, with amendments recommended before final approval.
